title: Mock v. Garland (2023)
summary: A final rule that abandons the concrete test proposed for comment in favor of an open-ended balancing test is not a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule and must be set aside under the Administrative Procedure Act.
notes:
Key line: In conclusion, it is relatively straightforward that the Final Rule was not a logical outgrowth of the Proposed Rule, and the monumental error was prejudicial. (Judge Jerry E. Smith)

Citation: 75 F.4th 563 (5th Cir. 2023).

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs and appellants were William T. Mock and Christopher Lewis, individual owners of pistols fitted with stabilizing braces; Firearms Policy Coalition, Inc., a nonprofit; and Maxim Defense Industries, L.L.C., a manufacturer of braces. The defendants and appellees were Attorney General Merrick Garland, the Department of Justice, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, and its Director Steven Dettelbach. The panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit consisted of Judges Jerry E. Smith, Stephen A. Higginson and Don R. Willett. Judge Smith wrote the opinion for the court.
sections.Material Facts: The National Firearms Act of 1934 and the Gun Control Act of 1968 impose registration, tax and transfer requirements on short-barreled rifles but not on pistols. In 2012 a federal firearms licensee asked ATF whether a stabilizing brace, a forearm strap for disabled or weaker shooters, turned a pistol into a rifle; ATF said it did not. On June 10, 2021, ATF published a proposed rule, 86 Fed. Reg. 30826, that would classify braced firearms using Worksheet 4999, a point system scoring objective design features. The agency received hundreds of thousands of comments, mostly negative. On January 31, 2023, ATF issued the final rule, 88 Fed. Reg. 6478, which discarded the point system in favor of a six-factor balancing test that considered, among other things, the weapon's weight and length, the surface area of the brace, marketing materials and community use as shown in online videos. Owners had until May 31, 2023 to comply before criminal penalties attached.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs sued in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas, No. 4:23-CV-95, raising Administrative Procedure Act and constitutional challenges and moving for a preliminary injunction. Judge Reed O'Connor denied the motion, concluding among other things that the final rule was interpretive and in any event a logical outgrowth of the proposal. The plaintiffs appealed and moved for an injunction pending appeal; when the district court did not rule promptly, a Fifth Circuit motions panel enjoined enforcement against the named plaintiffs on May 23, 2023, clarified on May 26. The merits panel heard the expedited appeal and, on August 1, 2023, reversed the denial of the preliminary injunction, remanded for the district court to decide the remaining injunction factors and the scope of relief, and maintained the injunction pending appeal for sixty days or until the district court ruled.
sections.Issue: Were the plaintiffs likely to succeed on their claim that the final rule violated the Administrative Procedure Act? Answering that required deciding two questions. First, is the final rule a legislative rule subject to the notice-and-comment requirements of 5 U.S.C. section 553, or an interpretive rule exempt from them, as the district court and the Government maintained? Second, if it is legislative, was the final rule a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule, so that interested parties had fair notice of its substance and a meaningful chance to comment, given that the proposal used a points worksheet and the final rule used a six-factor balancing test?
sections.Holding: The plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their APA claim. The final rule is legislative, not interpretive: it binds the public with the force of law, carries criminal consequences, and ATF itself invoked the notice-and-comment procedure and claimed legislative authority. The final rule is not a logical outgrowth of the proposed rule. The proposal told the public that ATF would apply a quantifiable point system to objective design features; the final rule replaced it with an indeterminate six-factor test that considers subjective and external matters and that commenters could not have anticipated or addressed. The error was prejudicial, so the rule must be set aside as unlawful or remanded for remediation. The district court's contrary order is reversed and the case remanded for the remaining preliminary injunction factors.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Smith first addressed the character of the rule. Interpretive rules merely advise the public of the agency's construction of a statute, while legislative rules create new rights or duties with the force of law. The final rule fits the second description: ATF invoked its rulemaking authority, imposed felony liability for noncompliance and described the rulemaking as legislative. Because the rule is legislative, section 553 governs, and under Long Island Care at Home v. Coke the final rule must be a logical outgrowth of the proposal so that the public receives fair notice of the subjects and issues. The court compared the two texts closely. The proposed rule promised an objective, points-based worksheet, and its preamble emphasized objective design features. The final rule abandoned the worksheet entirely and adopted six factors, some of which depended on how third parties marketed or used the weapon rather than on its design. A commenter who had addressed the point values or the thresholds of the worksheet would have found those comments irrelevant to the test finally adopted. The court rejected ATF's argument that mention of the same general subjects sufficed and that plaintiffs had to show which additional comments they would have filed, holding that the failure of notice itself established prejudice. Because a procedurally invalid rule cannot stand, the plaintiffs had shown a likelihood of success, and the remaining factors were left to the district court.

topics.lrs-o-logical-outgrowth: The panel divided over whether replacing the proposed worksheet with a six-factor test was adequately forecast; the majority decided likelihood of success rather than final merits.
topics.lrs-o-section-553: Logical outgrowth is the measure of whether § 553(b)'s notice requirement was satisfied by the proposed rule.

learning.separateOpinions: Two to one. Judge Willett concurred, joining the majority in full and adding that the six-factor test would likely fail constitutional scrutiny for vagueness even if it had been a logical outgrowth, since owners could not know in advance whether their braced pistols were rifles. Judge Higginson dissented, arguing that the final rule was a logical outgrowth because the proposal identified the same factors, that ATF was closing a loophole in a century-old registration regime, and that Judge O'Connor's denial of the injunction should be affirmed; he noted that the remand left the district court free to limit or deny injunctive relief.
